mappings.note: Both advocacy statements are true -- emotional health and empowering women through sport. Her advocacy is how the text presses its case past the disabled-equals-helpless assumption, C-2.2-LO-22.
She empowers women through ADVENTURE sports -- the choice of adventure over cooking, knitting or painting is the stereotype the item breaks, C-2.2-LO-22.
She provides equipment to athletes from POORER backgrounds -- a plain detail of her work with no stereotype or resilience argument attached, so C-2.2 competency rather than LO-22.
'Every setback is an opportunity to prove your STRENGTH' -- the chapter's resilience line, C-2.2-LO-21. Not LO-22: setbacks, not stereotypes.
The universal lesson -- focus entirely on our ABILITIES, with 'focus heavily on disabilities' as the trap option. C-2.2-LO-22 in one line.
Whom the chapter hopes to involve (the youth) -- recall of the closing section's audience, C-2.2 competency. The items asking WHY the youth matter are mapped to LO-10.
The future society hoped for -- inclusive and empathetic, against options that ignore or pity the disabled. The stereotype-breaking clause of C-2.2-LO-22.
Equality and DIGNITY, with 'pity' and 'sympathy' as the distractors -- the item turns on rejecting the pity frame, which is exactly what LO-22 covers.

The central theme of the summary -- overcoming challenges. Resilience as the chapter's spine, C-2.2-LO-21. (a) Gold medal (b) Silver medal (c) Bronze medal (d) Copper medal', which belong to a different item.
The event in which she medalled (shot-put) -- factual recall, C-2.2 competency.
Her Asian Games record -- the FIRST female para-athlete. Factual recall, C-2.2 competency; the items that ask what such firsts mean for attitudes are mapped to LO-10.
India's first female Paralympic medallist across ANY sport -- factual recall, C-2.2 competency.
Named among the top ten most EFFECTIVE para-athletes -- factual recall, C-2.2 competency.
Who named her (the International Paralympic Committee) -- factual recall, C-2.2 competency.
Which civilian award (Padma Shri) -- factual recall, C-2.2 competency.
The other award (Khel Ratna) -- factual recall, C-2.2 competency.

How society HISTORICALLY viewed disabled individuals (as completely helpless) -- the baseline attitude against which the chapter measures change, which is what C-2.1-LO-10 is for. Not LO-22, which is about how the text argues against that view; this item asks what the old view was.
What SHATTERS the helplessness stereotype -- her medals, not her speech or her writing. C-2.2-LO-22's stereotype clause, with the evidence named.
Competing globally proves para-athletes possess immense COMPETITIVE SPIRIT -- ability asserted against the assumption of incapacity, C-2.2-LO-22.

The Paralympics as a global STAGE -- the Games themselves as the instrument by which attitudes move, which is C-2.1-LO-10's subject. Not LO-20: 'stage' here is the platform, not stadium imagery placing the reader beside the athlete.

The Paralympics shifts focus from disability to ABILITY -- the phrase C-2.2-LO-22 is built on. DEFECT: the answer runs on into an unrelated dialogue (Siya and Tarun on para equestrian events), which belongs to the reported-speech exercise.

Part of the special-assembly notice exercise -- the answer supplies the VENUE ('the school auditorium'), which is one of the what/when/where/who slots C-1.3-LO-5 requires. DEFECT: the stem is a fragment of one blank ('The celebration will end with a _____ to encourage team work') while the answer answers a different numbered blank, so the item as stored cannot be marked.

How Sheetal Devi's achievement SETS THE TONE for the chapter -- a question about how the piece is constructed, so C-2.2 (critiquing form and style). Not C-2.1-LO-9, which asks the reader to classify the genre and contrast its purpose with a story's.

The role of willpower in para-athletes' lives -- looking beyond physical constraints, which is the ability-beyond-disability argument, C-2.2-LO-22. Not LO-21: no single incident is cited, the claim is general to the group.
Describe the tragic turn at twenty-nine -- the tumour, the surgery, the paralysis. A specific incident of adversity, C-2.2-LO-21.
The two paths open to her and the one she chose -- the decision that defines the resilience theme, C-2.2-LO-21. Not C-3.2: she made the choice, the student does not argue one.

Why her move into para-athletics is like a butterfly leaving the chrysalis -- struggle producing transformation, the overcoming-adversity strand of C-2.2-LO-21. Not LO-20, whose imagery is the stadium and the athlete in action.

The significance of Rio 2016 -- the breakthrough that completes the arc from paralysis to a historic silver. Incident-anchored resilience, C-2.2-LO-21, not bare recall, because the question asks for its significance.

Her other historic FIRSTS for Indian WOMEN in para-sport. A run of firsts is precisely how an account registers changing attitudes and access over recent decades, C-2.1-LO-10. The bare who-won-what recall items are kept at C-2.2.

How the IPC acknowledged her global impact -- naming her among the most effective para-athletes for her competing AND her advocacy. The advocacy is the stereotype-breaking work of LO-22; the plain who-named-her recall is mapped separately at C-2.2.
Which national awards honour her (Padma Shri and Khel Ratna) -- factual recall, C-2.2 competency.

How her medals shatter the HISTORICAL STEREOTYPES about disabled people -- LO-22's second clause stated in full, and the concept tag 'Breaking Stereotypes' agrees. DEFECT: 'NODIA' page furniture is embedded mid-answer.

How the Paralympic STAGE shifts GLOBAL PERSPECTIVES -- the Games as the recorded engine of attitude change, C-2.1-LO-10. Distinguished from the LO-22 items, which turn on one athlete's case against a stereotype.

How she uses her platform to help the government improve sport -- shaping INCLUSIVE policies for differently-abled athletes. Advocacy against the old assumptions, C-2.2-LO-22. Not C-2.1-LO-10: the item asks what she does, not how attitudes have moved.
The specific ways she uplifts women -- adventure sports, breaking gender AND disability barriers. Stereotype-breaking, C-2.2-LO-22.

How she supports underprivileged athletes -- supplying equipment so money is not the barrier. A comprehension detail about financial support rather than about ability or stereotype, so C-2.2 competency.

Why she stresses EMOTIONAL health alongside physical training -- mental fortitude as what carries a person through the darkest moments. The resilience strand, C-2.2-LO-21. Not LO-22: nothing about ability against disability is argued.

Interpret 'Every setback is an opportunity to prove your strength' IN THE CONTEXT OF HER LIFE -- the quote tied back to the tumour and the medal, which is LO-21's 'from specific incidents'. The earlier item that asks the same quote to be generalised beyond sportspeople was mapped to C-3.2 instead.
Why society should focus on abilities rather than disabilities -- the chapter's own argument, which is what C-2.2-LO-22 asks the student to explain.

Why the chapter targets the YOUTH -- to dismantle long-standing prejudice so the next generation's attitudes differ from the last. Attitude change over time, C-2.1-LO-10. Not LO-22: the argument is about who must change, not about what the text proves.

The ideal future society at the chapter's close -- inclusive, empathetic, free of prejudice. The endpoint of the attitude shift the account traces, C-2.1-LO-10. DEFECT: the answer runs into 'Click Here to Buy b...'.

Justify the title from the LIFE TRAJECTORIES of Sheetal Devi and Deepa Malik -- both arcs of adversity overcome, so C-2.2-LO-21 with the incidents supplying the warrant. Not LO-22: the title is about possibility, not about refuting a stereotype.

Write a diary entry AS Deepa Malik on the day she was told she would be wheelchair-bound. Writing in another's voice from their experience, C-1.2. Cited at competency level because this chapter's two C-1.3 LOs are a school notice and a spoken piece on empathy -- neither is a diary -- and CG-1 has no other outcomes.

Draft a morning-assembly SPEECH urging peers to shift from disability to ability and to build an EMPATHETIC environment, drawing on Dr Malik. C-1.3-LO-6 names exactly this: speaking briefly on empathy and sportsmanship with an example from the text. The best-fitting LO in the chapter for any composition item.

A congratulatory letter to Sheetal Devi on the Arjuna Award -- real-life social writing of the kind C-1.3 lists alongside condolence messages and invitations. Not LO-5 (a notice) and not LO-6 (a spoken piece), so competency level.

Compose a dialogue between Dr Malik and a young athlete she is equipping, on mentorship and passing on resilience. C-1.1 for the scripted exchange in a social setting, C-2.2-LO-21 because the content the dialogue must carry is the resilience theme.
